# Reading In Data (continued)

## Reading in a CSV file

::: callout-note
### CSV
Comma Separated Value. Different columns are separated by comma characters (`,`). Any field that contains a comma must be quoted.
:::
```{r}
#| include: false

library(readr)
library(dslabs)
path <- system.file("extdata", package="dslabs") 
files <- list.files(path, full.names = T) 
```

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

```{r} 
#| echo: true
library(readr)

carbon_df <- read_csv(files[3])         # <1> 
names(carbon_df) <- c("Year", "TotalC") # <2>
head(carbon_df)                         # <3>

```
1. Read in the third file in the list, which ends in `carbon_emissions.csv`
2. Rename columns to have shorter names
3. Look at the head (the first 6 rows, by default) of the object


:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: callout
### File contents
```{r}
#| echo: false

readLines(files[3])[1:10]
```
:::
:::
:::

## More Complicated CSVs

```{r}
#| echo: true

problems(olive_df) # <1>
```
1. When a CSV is not properly formatted, problems can pile up. Use `problems()` to see what R is complaining about. 


## More Complicated CSVs

```{r}
#| echo: true

readLines(files[8])[1:10] # <1>
```
1. When in doubt, look at the first few lines of the file. Count how many columns in several rows manually. Then come up with a hypothesis and a plan.

## CSV Trick: Separate the Names from the Data

```{r}
#| echo: true
olive_df <- read_csv(files[8],  # <1> 
                     col_names = FALSE, # <2>
                     skip = 1) # <3>
olive_names <- read_csv(files[8], col_names = FALSE, n_max = 1) # <4>
olive_names <- as.character(olive_names) # <5>
olive_names <- c("row", "RegionName", olive_names[-1]) # <6>
names(olive_df) <- olive_names # <7>
head(olive_df)
```
1. Read in the same file, but with additional arguments
2. Tell `read_csv` you're not providing column names
3. Skip the first line of the file
4. Read in only the first line of the file
5. Convert the table to a vector (a list)
6. Add names for the first two columns (row, RegionName) and remove the empty entry (`olive_names[-1]`). Put everything into the same vector using `c(...)`
7. Set the names of the table

## RStudio Projects

- Help you keep track of the files for a data science project
- File -> New Project -> New Directory 
  - Name your new project something descriptive
  - Put the project in sensible folder

- Move data into the project folder (into a `data/` subdirectory if multiple files)
- .R files in the project folder will find your data automatically without needing a file path. 

## Test Your Skills {.inverse}  

1. Navigate to [https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/cdo-web/search?datasetid=GHCND](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/cdo-web/search?datasetid=GHCND)
2. Select daily summaries
3. Search for Zip codes
4. Enter your Zip code (or 84321, Logan)
5. Search
6. Add a weather station to the cart 
7. Select Custom GHCN-Daily CSV as the output format
8. Use the default range
9. Custom options: Select all data types
10. Submit the request and wait for the email. Download the resulting CSV file.
11. Write code to read in the data.

## Teaching Rocks to do Math

::: incremental

- Remember you're talking to a rock [("dumb as a box of rocks...")]{.fragment .emph .cerulean-dk}
- You have to know a concept really well *before* you start programming
- Be extremely specific
- Consider what assumptions you are making. 
  - Try not to make them unless necessary.
  - If necessary, test to ensure they're met.

:::
